Marketable Treasury debt outstanding is now roughly $32 trillion and has grown substantially over the past two decades.3 Its uses are equally vast. Treasuries are the benchmark for pricing nearly every other dollar asset. They are the premier collateral in funding markets, a core holding for managing liquidity, a hedging instrument, and a global reserve asset. For the Federal Reserve, the Treasury market is central to how monetary policy works. When we set our policy rate, we influence overnight money market rates and the expected future path of short-term rates. These expectations affect Treasury yields further out the curve, which, in turn, affect borrowing costs for households and businesses. A mortgage rate, a corporate bond yield, a swap rate, each of these is built atop the foundation of Treasuries.

So, while we are one of several agencies with a stake in this market, the Fed is unique in that it has the operational expertise and funding capacity to intervene in the Treasury market if needed. The Fed has significant capabilities, but our remit is narrow. The FOMC has a responsibility to think carefully about when and how we should use our powerful tools. Any intervention would have an impact on our balance sheet, so it’s worth reviewing the three distinct roles that the Fed’s balance sheet plays: plumbing, policy, and financial stability. The first role, plumbing, is implementing day-to-day monetary policy to maintain the fed funds rate within the target range set by the FOMC. The second role is unconventional monetary policy.

The target range for the fed funds rate is our primary tool for achieving our dual mandate. However, asset purchases can provide additional monetary stimulus when the policy rate is constrained by the effective lower bound. The third role is financial stability. The Fed’s balance sheet can be used to provide liquidity to limit dysfunction that threatens the financial system and could impact the real economy. One example occurred in March 2020 when the Fed engaged in market-functioning purchases to ease stress in the Treasury market. When stress hits, there may be very little time to decide what principles to operate under or how to communicate them. It is better to identify the exit routes when you first enter the building than it is to draw up an evacuation plan as the building is filling with smoke.

First, although initially the purchases were driven by market-functioning concerns, economic conditions quickly shifted, necessitating purchases for policy accommodation. While I acknowledge that labeling the purchases is less important than the action itself,6 over time, the blurring of the two intentions made it difficult for market participants to understand how much was intended as policy accommodation and how much was to support market functioning. In the future, a clear delineation of intent would provide the public with insight into when intervention would no longer be needed and the conditions under which the FOMC would unwind the purchases. Second, it would be helpful if policymakers communicate clearly about how they determined the market stress was abnormal and intervention was needed and why the Federal Reserve was well placed to address these things.

Rather, it is exactly the kind of problem a central bank was designed to address. The goal would be to sharpen the distinction between market-functioning actions and unconventional policy actions. One approach could be to create an explicit market-functioning facility when needed, as the Bank of England did in 2022. The Bank of England’s model, however, doesn’t translate directly because the US doesn’t have separate monetary policy and financial policy committees. The US might be able to achieve a similar result by setting up a separate portfolio that would delineate financial stability purchases from unconventional monetary policy purchases. Additionally, our market structures are quite different. A key reason the Bank of England built its new facility was to transact directly with nonstandard counterparties in times of stress.

In the interest of starting that conversation, let me offer my own views on each. When to intervene First, the bar for intervention should be high. Periods of low liquidity are often associated with high volatility. But not every bout of low market liquidity calls for Fed action. Market functioning naturally adjusts to the level of volatility in the markets. When volatility rises, bid–ask spreads widen, and market depth thins.7 This is normal; as value-at-risk increases, dealers need to price for that greater risk. Fed action should be considered only when market functioning deteriorates beyond what should be expected given volatility levels and when this dislocation threatens monetary policy and financial stability goals. The market turbulence of early April 2025 is a good illustration.8 Amid extraordinary market volatility related to tariff news, liquidity deteriorated, and there was a risk that problems in the Treasury market would spill into mortgage and credit markets and from there into the real economy.

There was market chatter that the Fed should step in, but based on what I saw, liquidity conditions and other market-functioning metrics stayed within historical norms. Markets were strained but functioning.9 When poor liquidity conditions in volatile markets reflect fundamentals, it is not a problem the Fed can or should try to solve. A constellation of liquidity and market-functioning metrics and how they fit within a historical context can help policymakers gauge the risks to our monetary policy and financial stability goals. If there’s evidence that Treasury market dysfunction will spill into the real economy and that Fed action can address the problem, then intervention should be considered. What form intervention should take The presumption should be that the action is temporary and targeted, ideally with an exit strategy built in from the start.

Further, repos alone may not be effective in every situation. I doubt repos would have been enough in 2020. Thus, it may make sense to consider Treasury purchases if repo operations prove insufficient. A Treasury purchase program can be a critical tool, and its announcement can sometimes do much of the work itself. We saw this with several of the Fed’s credit market facilities in 2020. Uptake was relatively modest because the announcement alone restored confidence. Similarly, the Bank of England executed relatively small amounts of purchases. This shows that sometimes the sprinkler system’s coming on can inhibit panic and allow for a more orderly exit from a burning building. When the dislocation is caused by forced selling and financing support is insufficient, asset purchases may be necessary to relieve the pressure.

While each episode of stress is different, any program should aim to restore overall market functioning rather than target specific institutions. It should also be temporary, and holdings should be sold in a timely way once market financial stability is restored. Sprinklers can’t always put out the fire; sometimes you need a firefighter’s hose. How to communicate about it Finally, Fed communications should clearly distinguish policy actions from market-functioning actions. Clear communication is not merely a courtesy. Instead, it’s part of what makes the intervention work and part of what makes the exit credible. In the case of the Bank of England in 2022, for example, market-functioning purchases occurred during a tightening cycle. Helpfully, the Bank of England could rely on its [OFFICIAL] Policy Committee to decide and communicate the market-functioning actions, clearly distinguishing them from the actions of its Monetary Policy Committee.

The [OFFICIAL] Open Markets Desk monitors many such indicators daily and updates the committee at every meeting on financial market health. In recent years, there were periods when liquidity measures were poor, but market functioning remained orderly, and these measures remained in line with their historical relationship against volatility.
